chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Bunan ibn Muhammad, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from al-Sakuni, from Ja'far, from his father, from Ali (peace be upon him), that he used to reject the bequest (nahlah) in the will.

And whatever he acknowledged at the time of his death without proof or clear evidence, he rejected it. The meaning of this report is that we interpret it as: if the one acknowledging is suspected by the heirs, his acknowledgment is not accepted unless there is evidence. If no evidence stands, what he acknowledged is valid from his one-third share. This has been clarified by him (peace be upon him) in the narration of al-Halabi, Mansur ibn Hazim, and Isma'il ibn Jabir, whose mention was preceded. As for if he was healthy (not near death), what he acknowledged is from the principal of the wealth, like other debts, and that which reveals what we mentioned.

key_terms.إِقْرَار: Acknowledgment or confession, here referring to admitting a debt or gift.
key_terms.الدِّيُون: Debts, obligations owed by the deceased.
key_terms.النَّحْلَة: A bequest or gift made by a dying person, often to an heir, distinct from a will.
key_terms.بَيِّنَة: Clear evidence or proof, such as witnesses or documents.
key_terms.ثُلُث: One-third, the portion of the estate available for bequests after debts are paid.
key_terms.مُهْتَمًّا: Suspected or suspected of bias/influence by the other heirs.

ai.seo_question: How is a dying person's gift to an heir treated in Shia inheritance law if there is no witness?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi elaborates on the juristic principle of *iqrar* (acknowledgment) in the final illness, distinguishing between a bequest (*nahlah*) and debt based on the heir's credibility. The text clarifies that if the heir is suspected of undue influence (*muttaham*), the acknowledgment is limited to the one-third share unless corroborated by evidence; conversely, if the testator was healthy, it is treated as a full debt from the principal estate. This ruling ensures fairness in inheritance distribution by preventing heirs from manipulating the dying person's declarations.
